did.unittitle: Richard Hess Mullin-Palmer Tape Restoration Project Collection

physdesc.extent: 6 boxes : approx. 110 digital files ; 54 open reel tapes; 2 boxes of reels and packaging

did.abstract: The Richard Hess Collection chronicles the early history of tape recording in the United States. The tapes were assembled and reformatted by engineer and researcher Richard L. Hess from 2003 to 2008. At the end of World War II, Jack Mullin recovered examples of German tape recording technology and, along with film maker Bill Palmer, approached Ampex with the idea of manufacturing audiotape and players. Entertainer Bing Crosby was an enthusiastic early adopter, and this collection is largely recordings used in the production of his radio programs. Digital files are only available at Stanford Archive of Recorded Sound.
did.physdesc: Six boxes of audiotape are held by the Archive of Recorded Sound. The remainder of the collection is digital.

bioghist.head: Historical Background
bioghist.p: The Richard Hess Mullin-Palmer Tape Restoration Project Collection chronicles the widespread dissemination of one of the most important advances in sound recording technology: magnetic recording on tape. In 1945, a U.S. Army Signal Corp soldier named John T. "Jack" Mullin was assigned to recover examples of the latest German technology from the field. In a radio station, Mullin confirmed that the Germans had developed a system of sound recording and reproduction using paper and plastic tape. He returned to the United States with several reels of audio tape and two AEG Magnetophon brand reel-to-reel machines on which to play them. This was not the first time that this country was introduced to the technology (in fact, research was published widely in the 30s), but Mullin's initiative, along with the enterprise of filmmaker Bill Palmer, was essentially the avenue by which tape manufacturing began in the United States.

The story of Bing Crosby's involvement is familiar. In the late 1940s, Crosby hosted one of the most popular programs on radio: Philco Radio Time. Mullin and Palmer worked with Crosby to develop a tape machine. Harold Lindsay had attended a demonstration of the magnetophone at the May 16, 1946 meeting of the Institute of Radio Engineers (IRE, now IEEE) in San Francisco and along with Alexander M. Poniatoff, the founder of Ampex, sought out Mullin and Palmer for advice on developing a machine at Ampex. Ampex proceeded to develop its first model of tape recorder, the 200A, in 1947 (other companies, among them Brush, Rangertone, Orradio, and Presto, were also experimenting with magnetic recording with some success).

The adoption of Tape provided an ease of editing that appealed to Crosby and his producers, and allowed for more creativity in assembling programs. It was also judged in many trials to offer improved fidelity compared to disc and optical film. Because of the risk of tape failing during a live broadcast, shows were still aired from transcription discs; it was the recording and editing that was done with tape. The first program recorded on tape was broadcast October 1st, 1947, the start of the 1947-1948 season. The recordings in this collection consist largely of material used for the Philco program, including performances, outtakes, and advertisements. Among the other stars to be heard on the programs are Dinah Shore, Peggy Lee, Burl Ives, and Claudette Colbert.

The Richard Hess Collection is named for recording historian and audio engineer Richard L. Hess who assembled these tapes, transferred them, and provided detailed notes on both the content and its capture. Between 2001 and 2008, Hess drew from both public and private collections to construct a digital representation of the early days of magnetic recording in the United States.

processinfo.head: Processing Information
processinfo.p: Tape digtization information provided by Richard Hess:
"All tapes were reproduced on a Sony APR-5003 with Nortronics full-track mono play heads.
Digitization via an RME Multiface connected directly to the APR via a balanced patch bay.
Sampling at 96,000 samples per second, 24 bits.
The U.S. recorded tapes "Other Tapes" were reproduced at 30 in/s using the IEC/AES standard of 17.5 µs equalization.
The Tonschreiber tapes were reproduced using the same equalization but at about 28.5 in/s to match the 72 cm/s speed found in the Tonschreiber Technical Documentation.
The file containing the 11 reels was physically split so that 1-9 are on the 10.5-inch reel and 10-11 are on the 7-inch reel marked Crosby. #11 was originally supplied as a "misc" on a 3-inch reel.
Note DIN Hub Misc 2 was blank.

Misc 3 was transferred both as a full-track mono tape and on an NAB 2-track head on a Studer A810. This tape appeared to be recorded at 15 in/s and was reproduced using standard NAB equalization on both machines.
The Crosby Show mentions Leap Year and is also the week before Valentines Day, this would be early February 1948. Guest is Jimmy Stewart.
The portion of the Crosby show towards the centre of the hubless reel was badly damaged and folded. There are a few perturbations in playback that can be traced to this.

The very last section was on one of the 11 reels that had been in the paper bag. See my article in the 2001-07 Journal of the Audio Engineering Society "The Jack Mullin/Bill Palmer Tape Restoration Project" and these tapes are in the bag that Jim Wheeler is holding in the photo.
Transferred by Richard L. Hess Vignettes Media Aurora, Ontario Canada"

relatedmaterial.head: Related Collections
relatedmaterial.p: Stanford also holds the Ampex Corporation collection . Some material presented here is also available through the Pavek Museum of Broadcasting.

scopecontent.head: Scope & Contents
scopecontent.p: A significant portion of this collection (Reels 1-51) are reels of audio tape which are physically held at the Stanford Archive of Recorded Sound. However, the bulk of the collection consists of digital files, including transfers from those reels, as well as from tapes in several other collections not at Stanford. Prior to accession, each item (whether a physical reel or the digital file that was recorded from the tape) was assigned a reel number. There is also a series for all related documentation, including obituaries and tape transfer logs.

userestrict.head: Publication Rights
userestrict.p: Property rights reside with repository. Literary rights reside with creators of the documents or their heirs. To obtain permission to publish or reproduce, contact the Head Librarian of the Archive of Recorded Sound.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bing Crosby Show 1947-10-01. In the 1980s, while Ososke was working at Ampex in the Standard Tape Lab, he made a transfer of the original tape. This recording is very important historically as it was the first radio program to air nationally in the U.S. that was recorded and edited on tape. To assuage fears of the tape breaking during airing, the actual broadcast was from discs (called electrical transcriptions or ETs) made from the tapes.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Notes provided by Don Ososke:
"From Don Ososke 2009-09-01
Philco Radio Time with Bing Crosby Aired 1947-10-01
It is believed to have been recorded in August 1947. It was recorded in Hollywood, probably at what became the ABC Radio Network Station.
This was following the divestiture of the Blue Network from NBC (the Red Network) which became ABC.

Crosby did not want to perform his shows live at the time of broadcast. During the 1946-1947 season, Crosby and his team used disc recordings (electrical transcriptions) to record his shows. The Hooper ratings suffered due to the relatively poor quality of the ETs and this loss of quality was reportedly audible even on table top radios.

Tape recording became available at an opportune time for Crosby and his 1947-1948 season was the first nationally broadcast show to be recorded on tape. In the early days of the useage of tape, ETs were still made for the actual broadcast, as the engineers did not trust the old, frequently spliced German tape for actual on-air use.

Personnel on the show: Bing Crosby Jerry Colonna (introduction) John Scott Trotter (orchestra leader and arranger) Rhythmaires (Background Vocal Group) Ken Carpenter (announcer) Perry Botkin (guitar player) Peggy Lee (staff perfomer) Murdo McKenzie (technical director) John T. (Jack) Mullin (recording engineer)
Guest: Gary Cooper

1. Program Introduction 2. Where the Blue of the Night Meets the Gold of the Day (Bing Crosby Signature Intro, Crosby, Trotter, Botkin) 3. My Heart is a Hobo (Crosby, Trotter, Rhythmaires) 4. Philco Commercial (Carpenter) 5. Crosby introduces Peggy Lee 6. It Takes a Long Long Train with a Red Caboose to Carry My Blues Away (Lee, Trotter) 7. Patter - Crosby & Lee 8. Crosby introduces Gary Cooper 9. Mam'selle (Crosby, Trotter, Rhythmaires) 10. Chi-baba, Chi-baba (Crosby, Trotter) 11. Peg O' My Heart (Crosby, Trotter, Rhythmaires) 12. Patter - Crosby & Cooper 13. Ranchin on the Range (skit: primarily Crosby & Cooper with Lee and Trotter) 14. Philco Commercial (Carpenter) 15. You Do (Crosby, Trotter) 16. Program conclusion includes reprise of Blue of the Night (Crosby, Cooper, Trotter)"

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Standard Hour radio program, recorded at the War Memorial Opera House in San Francisco, 1953-01-25 (at least first half hour). Early stereo recording -- the normal broadcast would have been done in mono.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Description from Don Ososke:
"Notes provided by Don Ososke 2009-09-01
Recorded on January 1953-01-25, five days after Eisenhower was inaugurated. Recorded at the San Francisco War Memorial Opera House with the San Francisco Symphony Orchestra

This is NOT the recording of the radio broadcast but was a very early experimental recording made by Ampex engineers Russ Tinkham and Harold Lindsay. These engineers were interested in the stereophonic aspects of symphonic concert recordings and not capturing the announcer as one would for an actual broadcast.
Conducted by Alfred Wallenstein who was at the time the primary conductor of the Los Angeles Philharmonic.
The violin soloist was Arthur Grumiaux.

The tracks are: 1. Program Introduction 2. Beethoven Overture to the Creatures of Prometheus 3. Gian Carlo Menotti First Movement from symphonic work Apocalypse 4. Continuation of 3. 5. Third Movement of Apocalypse 6. Introduction of Grumiaux 7. Saint-Saens Introduction and Rondo Capriccioso 8. Standard Oil Commercial (3 mins) 9. Introduction of Kodaly Hary Janos Suite 10. Hary Janos Suite: Prelude; the Fairy Tale Begins 11. Viennese Musical Clock 12. Song 13. Song 14. The Battle and Defeat of Napoleon 15. Introduction of the movement Intermezzo 16. Intermezzo 17. Beginning of the Standard Hour Conclusion 18. Continuation of 17 and spoken tests"

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Jack Mullin demo tape from 1946. This is a copy of a high-quality tape transfer of the original of this material. The copy was made by Ososke when he worked at Ampex in the Standard Tape Lab in the 1980s. These are the demos that Mullin used in 1946 at the San Francisco IRE meeting that interested Harold Lindsay and eventually led to Mullin working with Crosby and Ampex developing tape recorders. This same material is on other tapes (Reels 75 and 77), but this may be the best copy, although 75 is the original done as a direct transfer.
